name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
title: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
answer: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how a model works, what data it uses, and what its outputs mean into language that a non-specialist can act on. The scope includes both formal regulatory examinations and ongoing client reporting, as well as internal reviews where fiduciary duty requires clear communication about model risk. It also covers the boundary between what a model can and cannot be said to do, so that explanations do not overstate certainty or hide known limitations.

sections.body: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how a model works, what data it uses, and what its outputs mean into language that a non-specialist can act on. The scope includes both formal regulatory examinations and ongoing client reporting, as well as internal reviews where fiduciary duty requires clear communication about model risk. It also covers the boundary between what a model can and cannot be said to do, so that explanations do not overstate certainty or hide known limitations.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work runs on documentation systems that record model versions, training data lineage, feature definitions, and approval history. Explanation tooling often includes sensitivity analysis libraries, feature importance calculators, and decision trace logs that can reproduce why a particular output was produced. Reporting pipelines assemble these records into model cards, validation summaries, and plain-language narratives for different audiences. The infrastructure must support auditability, so every explanation can be traced back to the exact model artifact and data snapshot that generated it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners typically separate global explanations, which describe how a model behaves across many cases, from local explanations, which describe why one specific decision was made. They use counterfactual testing to show what would have to change in an input for the output to change, and sensitivity analysis to show which features matter most. The work also involves writing model cards and fairness summaries that state intended use, known failure modes, and performance across relevant subgroups. Explanations are reviewed by model risk or compliance staff before they are shared, to catch technical jargon or unsupported claims.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on provenance: an explanation is only as strong as the record of where the model, data, and assumptions came from. Regulators and clients generally expect to see the version history, training window, and validation results behind any model they are asked to rely on. Risks include exposing proprietary model logic, creating a misleading impression of accuracy, or failing to disclose a material limitation that later causes harm. Fiduciary risk arises when an explanation is incomplete or selective in a way that a reasonable client or examiner would find material. Governance therefore requires that explanations be approved, versioned, and retained alongside the model artifacts they describe.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward explanations that are as auditable and standardized as financial statements, with clear links to model version, data lineage, and approval chain. Regulators are likely to ask for more granular provenance and real-time access to decision traces, while clients may expect plain-language summaries updated with each model release. There is also movement toward using simpler or inherently interpretable models for high-stakes decisions where the cost of a poor explanation is high. As model inventories grow, explanation workflows will need to scale without losing the human review that catches unsupported claims.
